intro: Chrome for medical billers on Mac is Google's browser running the payer portals and billing sites you use every day. It needs macOS 13 Ventura or later, and a few settings for passwords, printing and tabs make claims work faster. This guide covers those settings, the shortcuts that matter, and where Lazur fits on a claims screen.
tldr: Current Chrome needs macOS 13 Ventura or later. Check your version under Apple menu > About This Mac before anything else.
Use one Chrome profile per client or payer, and turn on the screen lock option for saved passwords at shared stations.
Print with ⌘P. If the print dialog does not fit your workflow, save the page through Google Drive.
Lazur points at things, guides you one click at a time and dictates text. It does not click buttons for you.
Ask your compliance lead before you use any AI tool on screens that show patient records.

blocks.text: Many billing jobs run in web tools. Eligibility checks, claim status pages and remittance downloads often live in a browser tab. That makes Chrome a work tool, not only a place to read email. Most of the advice below works even if you never try a voice assistant.
Check that your Mac runs current Chrome

Google's Chrome help page says you need macOS 13 Ventura and up to use Chrome on a Mac. Check your version before you blame a portal for a problem. Click the Apple menu > About This Mac and read the macOS version.

If your billing Mac runs an older system, it cannot run current Chrome. Ask your IT contact for an update plan. Do not try to force a newer browser onto an old system. A failed install wastes the morning you planned to spend on claims.
Keep Chrome updated and restore your tabs

Chrome updates in the background, but the update does not finish until you relaunch. Save any draft notes first. Then press ⌘Q to quit Chrome fully. Closing the window with the red button leaves Chrome running, so the update waits.

blocks.title: Get your tabs back
blocks.text: Open Chrome > Settings > On startup and choose to continue where you left off. Your claim tabs then return after each restart, so you can pick up the queue where you stopped.
Use one Chrome profile per client or payer

If you work for more than one practice, use a separate Chrome profile for each one. Each profile keeps its own history, saved passwords and extensions. Click your profile picture at the top right of the Chrome window to switch between them.

Worked example. Say you bill for a family practice and a surgery group. Create one profile named for each client. Sign in to each client's portals only inside its own profile. A wrong login in the wrong window is the mistake this setup prevents.

The common mistake is using the default profile for everything. Then personal email, client portals and old test logins share one history. The address bar suggests all of them when you type a few letters.
Save portal passwords in Chrome Password Manager

When you sign in to Chrome, saved passwords sync to your Google Account. Google's help page gives the path on a Mac as More > Passwords and autofill > Google Password Manager. Menu labels can change, so search Settings for passwords if you do not see that path.

Chrome has an option called Use your screen lock when filling passwords. It is off by default. Turn it on at any shared billing station. Chrome then asks for your Mac's screen lock before it fills a saved password.

blocks.title: Shared Macs need a rule
blocks.text: Ask the practice manager whether saved logins are allowed on a front-desk Mac before you store anything there. A saved login on a shared machine is available to everyone who uses that account.
Print claim pages and save them as PDF
To print in Chrome on a Mac, open the page, then press ⌘P or choose File > Print. Pick a destination, then click Print. Google's help page describes this flow for printing web pages.

Google's help does not give a separate Mac step for saving a PDF. Its PDF examples use Save to Google Drive or Drive for desktop. If the destination list does not fit your workflow, save the page through Drive and download it into your claim file.

items: Open the claim or remittance page in its own tab.
Press ⌘P to open the print dialog.
Choose a destination, such as a printer or Save to Google Drive.
Click Print, then confirm the file lands in the right claim folder.

blocks.text: The mistake to avoid is printing the whole portal page when you need one section. Press ⌘F to find the part you want. Then print only that page or range if the dialog offers the option. Less paper means less to sort later.
Keyboard shortcuts for payer portal work
These shortcuts cover most of the moves you make in a portal. Learn four first: ⌘L, ⌘F, ⌘T and ⇧⌘T. The rest come with practice, and each one saves a trip to the mouse.

blocks.text: Worked example. A remittance runs long, and you need one denial code. Press ⌘F, type the claim number, and Chrome jumps to the match. Copy the value, switch to your notes with ⌘Tab, then paste with ⌘V.

blocks.title: Incognito is not a shield
blocks.text: An incognito window keeps history off your Mac for that window. It does not hide your login or your activity from the payer's site. Use it for privacy on your Mac, not as a security step.

If a payer page is in another language, Chrome can translate it. See [how to translate a web page in Chrome](/how-to/translate-a-web-page-in-chrome) for the address bar, right-click and Settings steps.
Organize your claim queue with tab groups and bookmarks

Tab groups keep related work together. Right-click a tab and choose Add tab to new group. Name the group, pick a color, and keep one group for each stage of your queue, such as eligibility, submitted or waiting on the payer.
Bookmarks help too. Press ⌘D on each portal login page and file it in a folder named for the payer. Separate folders get you to any login in one click. One long flat list makes you scroll and guess.
The mistake to avoid is leaving every claim tab open all week. Old tabs hold stale data, and stale data causes errors. Close finished work with ⌘W, and reload any page before you trust what it shows.
Copy claim numbers without errors

Copying the wrong value costs more time than typing it again. Double-click a claim number to select it. Then check that the selection did not grab a trailing space or a line break. Paste with ⌘V, and read the value once more before you save the note.

Session timeouts add a second risk. Some portals log you out after a period of inactivity. A logged-out page can still show old data on screen. Reload the page, sign in again, and confirm the claim status before you act.
Where the time goes: claim denial and prior auth numbers

Numbers from the field help you decide where to start. They come from surveys and agency data, not from measurements in your office. Treat them as a starting point, then count your own work for a week.

The AMA's 2024 survey of 1,000 physicians found that practices complete 39 prior authorization requests per physician per week. Physicians and their staff spend an average of 13 hours a week on those requests. The same survey found that 89% of physicians say prior authorization somewhat or significantly increases burnout. Those figures cover physicians and staff, not billers alone.

Experian's 2026 State of Claims survey covered 204 healthcare staff who handle finance, billing, claims and collections. In that survey, 40% said at least one in ten claims is denied. Another 35% cited dominant manual processes as a reason to evaluate their technology. Those are shares of respondents, not denial rates measured in any one practice.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics counts about 200,700 medical records specialists who held jobs in 2025, and it projects 8% growth through 2035. Those workers handle records, and BLS does not list billing as a core duty. Use that figure as context, not as a count of billers.
Availity, a payer network company, says its network facilitates over 13 billion transactions annually. That is the company's own claim. It does not tell you what your office would save.
Use Lazur on a claims screen

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen.

Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time. It waits for each click before it moves on. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. You make every click, which keeps each submission in your hands.

Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Snippets, a personal dictionary and clipboard slots cover the phrases you repeat. Lazur's research tasks run in its own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension, then come back with a summary and a report.
What Lazur sees and where the data goes

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so Lazur can answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Read those rules yourself before you rely on them.

blocks.title: Patient data needs a check
blocks.text: This page does not say whether Lazur meets HIPAA requirements. Ask your compliance lead before you use Lazur on any screen that shows patient information.
How to phrase requests on a billing screen
Speak the way you would ask a coworker. Name the portal, the page and the goal. Lazur sees the screen only while you hold the shortcut, so describe what you need to find on it.

items: Name the screen. Say the payer portal and the page, not just this one.
Ask for one step at a time when Lazur is guiding you.
Ask Lazur to draft, then read the draft before you paste it anywhere.
Dictate call notes, but check every claim number on screen before you save it.

blocks.text: Clear questions get short, useful answers. Lazur reads the text on screen, so a readable page makes its answer better. Zoom in with ⌘+ when the text is too small to read.
Common mistakes billers make in Chrome

items: Using the default profile for every client, which mixes logins and history.
Closing the window with the red button and leaving Chrome running for days, so updates never finish.
Leaving screen lock off on a shared Mac that stores portal passwords.
Printing a full portal page when you need one section.
Trusting a dictated claim number without checking it on the screen.
Installing a random extension to fix a login. Ask IT first.

blocks.text: Each mistake costs a few minutes. Over a week, those minutes add up to a real block of time. Fix the profile and password habits first, since they carry the most risk to client data.
Edge cases: timeouts, unsupported browsers and Windows

Some portals list supported browsers in their help pages. Check that list before you blame Chrome. If a portal needs an older system or a browser plug-in, ask IT before you install anything. Do not run unknown downloads to fix a login.
Lazur runs on the Mac only. Windows is planned, not available. If your billing team uses Windows PCs, Lazur does not run there, so plan around that for now.
Timeouts cause a quieter kind of confusion. A logged-out page can look normal while it shows old data. Reload the page, sign in again, and check the claim status before you act on it.
Start with Lazur on a Mac you already use

Lazur has a Pro trial with no credit card. The trial starts when you first open the app. Check the [pricing page](/pricing) for current plan details before you choose one, then get the app from the [download page](/download).
Start with one portal and one task. Ask Lazur to point at one button. Then ask for one guided step. Build from there once the first session feels routine.
What to do next

items: Check your macOS version under Apple menu > About This Mac.
Quit Chrome with ⌘Q, relaunch it, and confirm your tabs return.
Create one profile for each client or payer you bill.
Turn on the screen lock option for saved passwords on shared machines.
Run one full claim session with the shortcuts from the table.
Download Lazur and ask it to point at one button on a portal page.

blocks.text: Start small. The first real session will teach you more than any checklist, including this one.

faq.question: Does Chrome run on every Mac?
faq.answer: No. Google's Chrome help page says you need macOS 13 Ventura or later to use Chrome on a Mac. Check your version under Apple menu > About This Mac. If your Mac is older, ask IT for an update plan before you change anything else.

faq.question: How do I print a claim page from Chrome on a Mac?
faq.answer: Open the page, press ⌘P or choose File > Print, pick a destination, and click Print. Google's help does not give a separate Mac step for saving a PDF, so use Save to Google Drive or Drive for desktop if you need a file.

faq.question: Where are saved passwords in Chrome on a Mac?
faq.answer: Google's help page gives the path as More > Passwords and autofill > Google Password Manager. On a shared Mac, turn on Use your screen lock when filling passwords, since that option is off by default.

faq.question: Can Lazur click buttons in a payer portal for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points at things, guides you one click at a time and waits for each click. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows billing PCs?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur is for the Mac, on Apple silicon and Intel. Windows is planned, not available, so Windows billing teams need another plan for now.

faq.question: Is Lazur safe to use near patient records?
faq.answer: This page cannot promise that. Lazur sends audio and screenshots to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. The page does not say whether Lazur meets HIPAA requirements, so ask your compliance lead first.

faq.question: Is there a free trial?
faq.answer: Lazur has a Pro trial with no credit card. The trial starts when you first open the app. See the pricing page for current plan details.
